case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Air Force’s submission of a hazardous-waste permit-renewal application to Guam EPA—without preparing NEPA review—constitutes “final agency action” reviewable under the APA and, if so, whether NEPA applies or is displaced/functionally replaced by RCRA’s permitting scheme.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 704 (final agency action); National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C) (EIS requirement for major federal actions); Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) permitting framework (as the asserted alternative statutory scheme).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Air Force and related federal defendants) argue that the challenged step is not a reviewable “final agency action” because the permit-renewal application itself has no direct legal consequences until (and unless) Guam EPA acts on it; it is at most an interlocutory submission that merely informs a later, legally operative decision by a different sovereign. They analogize to cases like Franklin and Dalton where agency reports/recommendations were not final because an intervening actor’s approval was required for legal effect. Petitioners further contend that, even if reviewable, NEPA should not apply in this RCRA-permitting context because RCRA’s permitting procedures displace NEPA or serve as NEPA’s functional equivalent, making NEPA analysis superfluous and creating duplicative process.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Prutehi Guahan) maintains that the Ninth Circuit correctly found final agency action because the Air Force’s decision to submit a specific permit-renewal application and waste-disposal plan represents the consummation of the federal agency’s decisionmaking on the proposed course of action and has meaningful legal and practical consequences in the regulatory regime governing the facility. Respondent also argues there is no genuine circuit split warranting Supreme Court intervention and that the Ninth Circuit properly applied Bennett’s two-part finality test. On the merits, respondent contends NEPA applies because Congress did not clearly displace NEPA in RCRA permitting and RCRA’s procedures are not the functional equivalent of NEPA’s environmental review requirements, so NEPA compliance remains required for the relevant federal action.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counter: that the Air Force’s application is a completed federal commitment that predictably channels Guam EPA’s process and forecloses meaningful NEPA review if we wait. But under Bennett’s second prong, as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, practical or procedural influence is not enough; the challenged federal act must itself determine rights or obligations or produce legal consequences, and here those consequences arise only if—and as—Guam EPA independently grants, denies, or conditions a permit. Justice Jackson’s attempt to distinguish Franklin and Dalton because they involved intra-Executive recommendations does not overcome their core finality principle: where an intervening decisionmaker supplies the operative legal effect, the antecedent submission is not “final agency action” under § 704. On a minimalist approach, we should decide only finality and avoid the broader NEPA–RCRA displacement and functional-equivalence questions until there is a legally operative federal action to review.

Spear’s second prong is textual and legal: the challenged federal action itself must determine rights or obligations or produce legal consequences. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, any binding permission, prohibition, or conditions arise only if—and as—Guam EPA exercises its independent sovereign discretion to grant, deny, or condition the permit, which is the same intervening-decisionmaker problem identified in Franklin and Dalton. Under an originalist/textualist reading of APA § 704, treating ordinary submissions to a separate regulator as “final” would collapse the statutory finality limit into a pragmatic-effects test untethered from legal consequence. Because there is no final agency action, NEPA merits and any NEPA–RCRA displacement questions are premature.

Because review is premature at the application stage, NEPA-based challenges can be brought, if at all, when there is a reviewable federal action with concrete effects; and in any event the workability concerns and statutory coherence of running NEPA in parallel with RCRA’s detailed permitting regime counsel against treating the application itself as the trigger. On that narrower APA ground, I would reverse without needing to resolve the full extent of any NEPA displacement by RCRA.

Spear an action is final only if it both consummates the agency’s decisionmaking and is one from which “legal consequences will flow.” The Air Force’s submission of a permit-renewal application to Guam EPA initiates a separate sovereign’s permitting process and does not itself determine rights or obligations; any binding consequences arise only if and when Guam EPA issues, denies, or conditions a permit, making this case akin to nonfinal recommendations or steps in a process rather than a consummated federal decision. Treating an asserted NEPA defect as the source of “finality” would invert § 704 and resemble the sort of “programmatic” or in-process challenge rejected in Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation. Because there is no final federal agency action here, courts lack APA jurisdiction to compel NEPA compliance at the application stage, and separation-of-powers principles counsel against expanding judicial review beyond Congress’s finality requirement.
